content: CD63 antigen is a protein encoded by the CD63 gene in humans. This protein is predominantly associated with the membranes of intracellular vesicles, although its expression on the cell surface can be induced under certain conditions. Function The protein encoded by the CD63 gene belongs to the transmembrane 4 superfamily, also referred to as the tetraspanin family. Members of this family are typically cell-surface proteins characterized by the presence of four hydrophobic domains. These proteins are involved in signal transduction processes that regulate various cellular functions, including development, activation, growth, and motility. CD63 is a cell-surface glycoprotein that forms complexes with integrins and may serve as a marker for blood platelet activation. A deficiency in this protein has been linked to Hermansky-Pudlak Syndrome, and the gene has also been implicated in tumor progression. Additionally, alternative polyadenylation sites and alternative splicing of this gene result in multiple transcript variants encoding different protein isoforms. Allergy Diagnosis CD63 is a reliable marker for flow cytometric quantification of in vitro activated basophils, which is used in the diagnosis of IgE-mediated allergies. This diagnostic test is commonly referred to as the basophil activation test (BAT). Research Initial studies using deletion and point mutants of CD63 focused on the role of its C-terminus, which contains a putative lysosomal-targeting/internalization motif (GYEVV). Mutations in the C-terminus led to increased surface expression and decreased intracellular localization compared to wild-type CD63. Antibody-induced internalization was reduced in C-terminal deletion mutants and abolished in specific point mutants (G→A and Y→A), highlighting the critical role of these residues in internalization. CD63 is extensively and variably glycosylated, with the EC2 region containing three potential N-linked glycosylation sites (N130, N150, and N172). Mutants N130A and N150A exhibited intracellular localization and internalization patterns similar to wild-type CD63. However, the N172A mutant predominantly localized to the cell surface and showed reduced internalization. A mutant lacking all three glycosylation sites was highly unstable. It has been speculated that the reduced internalization of the N172A mutant may result from altered interactions with cell-surface molecules. Immunoprecipitation experiments provided some evidence of a 100 kDa protein associating with CD63 N172A, but this finding was inconsistent. However, co-internalization studies demonstrated an association between wild-type CD63 and β2 integrin (CD18), suggesting that interactions with CD63 may influence the trafficking and function of β2 integrins. Recent research has shown that CD63 expression positively correlates with the invasiveness of ovarian cancer. In cell biology, CD63 is frequently used as a marker for multivesicular bodies, which are enriched with this protein. Interactions CD63 has been shown to interact with CD117 (c-Kit) and CD82, among other proteins.
